title: Aggrega Wasm Provider Render Socket
description: The wire shapes a Provider render plugin socket consumes and emits. A Provider guest renders one IR node into output files on its render_node export (RenderNodeInput to RenderNodeOutput), and optionally merges the per-node outputs at one boundary into a single assembled artifact on its assemble_boundary export (AssembleBoundaryInput to AssembleBoundaryOutput). AssembleBoundaryOutput carries the assembled files and any diagnostics; where each contributor's files sit is declared once on the guest's describe() contract rather than on this reply. A guest may also declare an optional validate_node_input export that structurally checks a node's resolved input before render dispatch: it consumes the same RenderNodeInput projection render_node receives and returns a ValidateNodeOutput carrying only diagnostics — a halt-severity diagnostic stops the build loudly, a warn-severity diagnostic surfaces to the build result. A guest whose target bounds or restricts the names it accepts may also declare an optional name_bound export, which the host asks before it settles a node's component identity: it consumes a NameBoundInput carrying one proposed name and returns a NameBoundOutput carrying one verdict per kind of name the guest would derive from it. A verdict carries a constraint — usable, or bounded to a shorter length — and never a name the guest built, so the knowledge of what the target accepts stays in the guest. Separately, a guest whose target derives a name of its own for the resources it renders — from author-supplied source, or from a workload it synthesizes — may declare an optional rendered_name export, which the host asks so a Recipe author can read that name and publish an address built from it: it consumes a RenderedNameInput carrying the identities the target derives from and the input kinds the node's Recipe declares, and returns a RenderedNameOutput carrying the name the guest itself will render under, or no name where it derives none. The two exports are opposite directions of one subject and neither stands in for the other — name_bound asks the guest to judge a name the host proposes, while rendered_name reports a name the guest composed, which the host carries without reading. A guest may also declare carve and reassemble, which carve its own output into addressable units for a pipeline step and splice the patched units back, and link_publish and link_resolve, which wire a uses edge whose ends assemble into different dispatch groups. Each payload's shape is the definition its export names: the x-aggrega-exports table maps every export the host calls a guest with — carve and reassemble included — to the definition of its input and the definition of its output, each as a JSON Pointer into this document's $defs, so a tool validating a payload looks its definition up there. The document root declares no shape of its own, because one document can be a valid payload of several exports (an empty object is a valid answer from validate_node_input, name_bound and rendered_name alike). The guest returns each output file's serialized bytes; the host writes them verbatim and runs no serializer, so determinism is the guest's responsibility: identical input must produce identical bytes. The Go, Rust and TypeScript payload types are generated from this schema into the plugin-ABI packages, so the three languages read and write one wire; a guest imports them from those packages, or through its plugin kit where the kit re-exports them.

RenderNodeInput.description: The payload a Provider guest receives on its render_node export: the per-node IR projection the guest renders, the render-time context, the pre-evaluated inputs the node's bound Recipe declares — an acquired-source listing, a workload, an artifact set — each present only when that Recipe declares it, and the entries naming rendered units the guest leaves out of a source render.

context.description: The render-time context the host hands the guest, carried as the bytes of its JSON document; this schema leaves the object undeclared. It is the context a pipeline step of the same node receives, plus the indentation width: parameters, the Release's parameter values sorted by name, absent when there are none; annotations, the node's annotations split by where each was written into aggregate, release and catalog, each absent when empty; boundary, the boundary the node sits in: name, path (its segments), sync_wave (absent when 0), directory, sub_directory (absent when there is none) and annotations (the set the Release's boundaries cascade down to the node, with its own Release entry's layered last; absent when empty); and yaml_indent, the render-wide indentation width the guest serializes its output at. The render of a boundary-scope FeatureRecipe, which has no host component, receives the context its pipeline step receives, plus yaml_indent: parameters; annotations carrying the release bucket alone, which is the boundary's own annotation set; and a boundary carrying its name, path and that same set as its annotations. The well-known aggrega.ai/* annotations are read from the aggregate bucket with the release bucket written over it, so a key both carry takes the Release's value; a standard-library provider reads them from that layered set and never from the catalog bucket, so a catalog value never decides one, and a boundary-scope FeatureRecipe, whose context carries no aggregate bucket, renders by its boundary's values rather than by any component's.

source_listing.description: The generic enumeration of the acquired source the host hands the guest for a sourced provider: the source root, whether that root is a directory, and the sorted root-relative entries under it. The host reads no file content here — it lists names only. The guest applies its own resolution logic over the listing and asks the host to pack a chosen selection through the pack-source host function, so all per-provider source-resolution intelligence lives in the guest. Present for sourced providers; absent otherwise.

workload_projection.description: The pre-evaluated workload the host hands the guest to synthesize provider-native manifests from; present when the bound Recipe declares a workload rather than a chart source, absent otherwise.

artifacts_projection.description: The pre-evaluated artifact set the host hands the guest to place into the node's output, present when the bound Recipe declares artifacts. The host has already read each entry's source, evaluated it as a Go template against the render context, and computed the build-provenance key sets; the guest decides the output format, the provenance placement, the on-disk path, and the final bytes. Absent when the node declares no artifacts.

omits.description: The entries naming rendered units the guest leaves out of this node's output, in the order the author declared them. Each entry arrives resolved, its fields plain strings, and an entry that does not apply to this build is not carried. What an entry's kind, name, namespace and subchart select is this provider's own documented contract, not this socket's: the guest matches every entry against what it rendered in its own format's terms, leaves each unit an entry matches out of everything it returns — its files, the names it declares in derived_keys and the facts it reports in render_facts — and reports in the output's omitted how many units each entry matched. The entries accompany a source listing and no other input: a render of a synthesized workload or of an artifact set never carries them. Absent when there are no entries, and a guest handed none renders exactly as it would if the field did not exist.

IRNodeProjection.description: The per-node IR data a Provider guest renders — a bounded projection of the full IR node carrying the per-node identity and the provenance the guest stamps onto every emitted manifest: its id, type, resolved recipe, values, whether a values mapping produced those values, feature attachments, the sensitivity marking over its rendered keys and over the values as a whole, outbound uses edges, boundary path, sync wave, Recipe identity, component-id override, derived-name basis, and build provenance. The identity and the derived-name basis are two carries because they answer two questions — what a resource belongs to, and what an author's own source renders against — and a Feature attachment delivering source its author wrote is where the two answers differ. Source-file content is not carried here; it travels separately in the source projection. Every key set here has a fixed order — features and uses in author order, values and the sensitivity marking in sorted key order — so the wire payload is byte-identical across runs of identical input.

id.description: The node's absolute id within the topology graph.

type.description: Declared and deliberately withheld: the host always emits this as the empty string. The node's component-type label is opaque metadata rather than a behavior switch, so carrying it here would only invite a guest to branch on it. A guest reads an empty string and must not read that as a node whose component type is unset. (The boundary-assembly node shape carries a type of its own, for a different purpose.)

resolved_recipe.description: Declared and deliberately withheld: the host always emits this as the empty string. The bound Recipe's identity already reaches the guest as the recipe name and version it stamps into provenance, so the resolved URI adds nothing a guest renders from. A guest that needs to attribute output to a Recipe reads those provenance fields instead.

values.description: The node's rendered values dictionary, the key set the guest renders from. Keys arrive in sorted order, not author order, and that sorting is what makes the payload byte-identical across runs of identical input; a guest needing any other ordering imposes it itself.

features.description: The node's feature attachments keyed by feature alias, carrying the same per-node feature-attachment shape the IR carries. Each entry carries the attachment's values, infra and inject mapping alongside its derived sensitivity marking, so a guest reads whether an attachment handles declared-sensitive material from the payload alone. Preserves author order so the payload is byte-identical across runs of identical input. Opaque at this schema layer; the guest reads the feature-entry shape through the IR wire contract.

sensitive_rendered_keys.description: Rendered keys whose identity is recovered from a datum an author declared sensitive, each mapped to the declaration it inherited that sensitivity from. Travels host to guest on the render input — the opposite direction from the names a guest declares on the render output. What a key names follows the shape this payload carries: on a payload carrying the node's values it is one of that map's keys; on a payload carrying a workload it names an entry in the workload's own attachment maps, where the node's values are empty. A key is present only where the recovery is exact, joining a declaration to a rendered identity with nothing read out of the key's own text and no per-node or per-attachment marking spread across individual keys. A key a template invented is therefore absent, because no declaration names it: the output keys of a recipe's valuesMapping, and the content of an artifact, are template-authored, so neither yields a key here — whether such a payload was produced from a value declared sensitive is carried instead by sensitive_values, and by an artifact entry's own sensitive_content. Absence therefore states that no key's identity could be recovered, never that nothing on this payload carries sensitive material — a guest that reads an absent key as permission to display or emit a value in the clear has read it backwards. Keys arrive in sorted order, which is what makes the payload byte-identical across runs of identical input.

sensitive_values.description: True when the values this payload carries were produced by a template that reads a value an author declared sensitive, or a value traced to one: a Recipe's or a FeatureRecipe's valuesMapping, a single template whose output keys and values are its own invention, so no key of that output can be traced back to the datum it came from and the whole map is marked instead. It is read from the template's own references against the declarations — a reference reaching a declared value, the template handing on the whole of its data, or a template that does not parse all count — and never from a value's content or a key's name. A guest composing text a person reads, a refusal or a warning, keeps every value of the node's values out of that text when this is true, and keeps out the value under any key sensitive_rendered_keys names whether or not it is: the two compose, one naming the keys whose identity is recovered exactly and this one covering the map where none can be. Absent when no such template read such a value, which includes values that are the declared leaves themselves, marked per key in sensitive_rendered_keys instead, and absent on a payload carrying no values. Absence never states that no value is sensitive.

values_mapped.description: True when the values this payload carries are the output of the bound Recipe's or FeatureRecipe's valuesMapping, rather than the node's values handed on as the author wrote them. A guest whose own contract binds to the inputs its source declares only the values a mapping produced reads this, and leaves values written for something else, such as the Recipe's artifacts, unread; a guest that binds the node's values to its source however they were produced does not read it. It records how the values were produced and is never derived from a key's name or a value's content. Absent where no valuesMapping ran, and on a payload carrying no values.

uses.description: Declared and deliberately withheld: the host never populates this, so the map is absent from every render payload. An outbound edge is consumed before dispatch — the edge's published values are rehydrated into the node's own inject pipe, which the Recipe has already evaluated into the values and workload the guest receives — and a guest assembling a boundary receives the edge list on its own input instead. Were it populated it would key the node's outbound uses edges by socket alias, each carrying that socket's ordered target node ids in author order.

boundary_path.description: The node's boundary path, stamped as the aggrega.ai/boundary-path annotation on every emitted manifest that carries a metadata block.

sync_wave.description: The deployment wave this node inherited from its containing boundary (default 0; negative permitted), carrying the value the IR node holds as `sync_wave`. What a guest does with it is the guest's own choice, and recording the value and ordering on it are independent rather than alternatives — a guest may do either, both or neither. Among the standard-library providers: `helm` and `helm-chart` emit it as an `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` annotation on every rendered resource, and additionally as `helm.sh/hook-weight` on a resource the chart already marks as a Helm hook; `compose` both records it as a service label and orders the services of the file it renders into, through `depends_on` between them; `cloudformation` orders provisioning of the assembled stack, declaring every resource in a wave to depend on the resources of the wave before it; `terraform` orders the module blocks of the root configuration a boundary assembles into, declaring every module in a wave to depend on the modules of the wave before it, and also records it with the node's build provenance.

recipe_name.description: The bound Recipe's name, paired with recipe_version to form the aggrega.ai/recipe-uri annotation; when either half is empty the annotation is not stamped.

recipe_version.description: The bound Recipe's version, paired with recipe_name to form the aggrega.ai/recipe-uri annotation; when either half is empty the annotation is not stamped.

label_component_id.description: The Kubernetes-safe component identity — what a resource this node emits BELONGS to, which is what provenance records and what a selector queries. When non-empty it overrides the node id as the app.kubernetes.io/name and aggrega.ai/component-id label value; empty means the node id is already label-valid and is used directly. It is carried for every resource a Feature attachment emits, whatever way the attachment delivers them, so an attachment's resources are distinguishable from its host component's by label alone. What a guest derives its own names from is a separate carry, derived_name_basis, and the two answer different questions.

derived_name_basis.description: The identity a guest derives its own names from — the release name a chart installer's templates read, which such a guest may also name the resources it synthesizes for a component after, and the prefix on the files a source render emits. Empty means the node id is used directly, which is the value for an ordinary component and for a per-component Feature attachment: an attachment delivering a chart or a fragment its author wrote renders it against the HOST component's name, because the author's own templates name resources after that name and a different one would rename resources already deployed. A node whose id carries marker syntax a target's name alphabet refuses carries this explicitly instead, so the name a guest derives stays one the target accepts. It is deliberately separate from label_component_id: a guest that BUILDS resources for a Feature attachment rather than rendering its author's source names them after the identity, so the attachment's own resources cannot collide with its host's, while the name an author's source renders against stays put. The two carry the same value wherever a node's identity is also what its source renders against.

output_labels.description: The recipe-author-declared output labels the guest stamps onto every emitted manifest alongside the build-identity provenance, keyed by label name. Two authored blocks merge into this one map: the literal key-value pairs a recipe writes in `outputLabels`, and one entry for each key a recipe names in `outputComponentLabels`, whose value is read from that key on the rendered component's own labels — so a promoted value follows the component it came from rather than being repeated in the recipe. Both blocks are disjoint from the provenance keyspace by load-time validation (no aggrega.ai/ or app.kubernetes.io/ key), so stamping never collides with a provenance label. A promoted key the component does not declare stamps nothing and raises an advisory rather than an empty label. A guest whose output is not Kubernetes YAML translates them onto its own label surface (Compose service labels) or ignores them.

provenance.description: The build-identity provenance the guest stamps onto every emitted manifest as aggrega.ai labels.

NodeProvenance.description: The build-identity provenance for one node — the compiler, aggregate, and environment identity the guest stamps onto every emitted manifest as aggrega.ai labels. Each field elides when empty, so a partial identity stamps only the labels it carries.

compiler_version.description: The compiler version, stamped as the aggrega.ai/compiler-version label when non-empty.

aggregate_name.description: The aggregate name, stamped as the aggrega.ai/aggregate-name label when non-empty.

environment.description: The environment name, stamped as the aggrega.ai/environment label when non-empty.

provider_name.description: The bare provider kind, stamped as the aggrega.ai/provider label when non-empty.

provider_version.description: The resolved provider-rendering plugin version, stamped as the aggrega.ai/provider-version label when non-empty.

RenderNodeOutput.description: The payload a Provider guest returns from its render_node export: the serialized bytes of each output file the guest emitted, the names it derived into each of its own key spaces, the facts it reports about what it emitted, how many rendered units each omit entry it was handed matched, and any diagnostics the guest raised while rendering. The guest returns each file's serialized bytes; the host writes them verbatim and runs no serializer. Determinism is the guest's responsibility: identical input must produce identical bytes.

files.description: The output files the guest emitted, in emission order. Each names its on-disk path and carries the serialized bytes the host writes verbatim.

derived_keys.description: The names the guest derived while rendering this node, keyed by the key space it derived them into, each space carrying its names in derivation order. A guest that derives the name its output addresses a resource by has put that name inside the file bytes the host writes verbatim, where the host cannot see it; declaring it here is how the guest asks the host to confirm no two derivations landed on one name. The host compares declared names for equality within one declared space and does nothing else — it does not parse a name, does not learn what a space or a name means, and never derives one itself. Two contributors to the same assembled output that declare the same name in the same space halt the build, and the halt names the space, the name, and both contributors. Both the space names and the names within them are the guest's own vocabulary: a guest wanting uniqueness across a narrower or wider scope than one assembled output expresses that scope in the space name it declares. Preserves declaration order so the payload is byte-identical across runs of identical input. Absent when the guest derives no names it wants checked, which leaves the check inert for that guest.

render_facts.description: Facts the guest reports about what it emitted for this node, in the order the guest lists them. Each fact pairs a name with a value, and both are the guest's own vocabulary: which facts a provider reports, what each name means and what its entries hold are part of that provider's documented contract, not of this socket's. Every fact's value is a list, even when it holds one entry: the host refuses a fact whose value is anything else, naming the provider and the fact, and halts the build. That is the one thing the host learns about a value. It keys facts by name and hands each list to the templates that read it, joining the lists of one name reported by more than one render of the same node in the order those renders ran, and it never learns what a name or an entry means or derives a fact itself — so a provider can report something only its own format knowledge can see, such as a property of the documents it wrote, without the host learning that format. Reporting facts never changes what is written: the files the host writes are the files the guest returned, whether or not facts accompany them. The guest lists its facts in a fixed order so the payload is byte-identical across runs of identical input. Absent when the guest reports nothing, which is a complete answer rather than a missing one.

omitted.description: How many rendered units each entry of the input's omits matched: one count per entry the guest was handed, in the same order, each the number of units that entry matched whether or not another entry also matched them. A count of zero is a complete answer — the entry matched nothing the guest rendered. The counts are all the socket carries back about what was left out: the units themselves are simply absent from what the guest returned. Absent when the guest was handed no entries.

diagnostics.description: Diagnostics the guest raised while rendering. Each element is the shared Wasm-plugin diagnostic shape.

error.description: A failure message set when the guest ran but could not complete the operation; absent on success. It is distinct from any diagnostics the output carries: diagnostics report issues found during a run that still produced a result, while error reports that the operation itself did not complete. The host surfaces a present error as a failed plugin invocation.

condition_code.description: The descriptive, machine-matchable identity of the condition the failure names — the code the condition is registered under, in the same open set the compiler registers its own halting conditions in, and not a member of the closed host-function error-code catalog a reply envelope's hostfunc_error_code draws from. Set beside the human error message; absent on success, and absent when the guest names no such condition. A guest that halts reports here the identifier of the condition its message names, so a consumer branches on it instead of recovering an identity by reading the message. The host resolves this identifier against the conditions the compiler declares and publishes the resolved condition's own identifiers on the structured diagnostic, so a code that reaches a reader always resolves; an identifier naming no such condition, or one the numbering has retired, halts the build. A guest with no precise condition to name reaches instead for one of the generic plugin-failure conditions the compiler declares for the purpose, and puts the specifics in its own message. This identifier and condition_short_code are reported together, because they name one condition in two forms: a guest that sets one and not the other has named a condition the host cannot resolve, and the host then reports its own generic plugin-failure condition instead while the message still carries the whole failure.

condition_short_code.description: The compact identifier of the same condition — the letter E and four digits, the form a reader quotes, searches for and pastes into a report — set beside the human error message; absent on success, and absent when the guest names no such condition. The host prints it in the bracketed head of the diagnostic it renders for this failure, so a condition a guest raises is quotable exactly as one the compiler raises is. The host resolves the value against the conditions the compiler declares rather than carrying it on trust: a value naming no such condition, a value the numbering has retired, or a spelling the registration does not carry halts the build and quotes the offending value, with the guest's own message still reported. It is reported together with condition_code, for the reason stated there.

ValidateNodeOutput.description: The payload a Provider guest returns from its optional validate_node_input export: the diagnostics raised by a structural check of the node's resolved input. The export consumes the same RenderNodeInput projection render_node receives and emits no files — it only reports diagnostics. A halt-severity diagnostic stops the build loudly, naming the node and provider; a warn- or info-severity diagnostic surfaces to the build result without changing rendered output. An empty diagnostics list means the input passed the structural check.

diagnostics.description: Diagnostics the guest raised while validating the node's input. Each element is the shared Wasm-plugin diagnostic shape. Empty when the input passed the structural check.

error.description: A failure message set when the guest ran but could not complete the operation; absent on success. It is distinct from any diagnostics the output carries: diagnostics report issues found during a run that still produced a result, while error reports that the operation itself did not complete. The host surfaces a present error as a failed plugin invocation.

Set beside the human error message; absent on success, and absent when the guest names no such condition. A guest that halts reports here the identifier of the condition its message names, so a consumer branches on it instead of recovering an identity by reading the message. The host resolves this identifier against the conditions the compiler declares and publishes the resolved condition's own identifiers on the structured diagnostic, so a code that reaches a reader always resolves; an identifier naming no such condition, or one the numbering has retired, halts the build. A guest with no precise condition to name reaches instead for one of the generic plugin-failure conditions the compiler declares for the purpose, and puts the specifics in its own message. This identifier and condition_short_code are reported together, because they name one condition in two forms: a guest that sets one and not the other has named a condition the host cannot resolve, and the host then reports its own generic plugin-failure condition instead while the message still carries the whole failure.

The host prints it in the bracketed head of the diagnostic it renders for this failure, so a condition a guest raises is quotable exactly as one the compiler raises is.
